newsitem.title: USA: Precious metals end higher led by platinum.
newsitem.headline: Precious metals end higher led by platinum.

text.p: Precious metals prices ended mostly higher Thursday led by platinum, which rose due to the five-month-old suspension of exports by Russia, the world's largest supplier of platinum and related metals.
Palladium eased slightly from Wednesday's levels, the highest in 17 years. Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and about 20 percent of its platinum.

"White metals were the star of the show, but even silver benefitted from the strength and gold looks again to be finding support around $340 an ounce," said Chase Manhattan managing director for global commodities, Dinsa Mehta.

July platinum jumped $25 to a new high of $436.60 an ounce at the New York Mercantile Exchange, while spot platinum was quoted around $446 an ounce after being fixed in London at $440, the highest since September 1995.

The active September palladium contract rose 35 cents to $173.15 an ounce. In the spot market, palladium was around $213.15, compared with the London fix of $235 an ounce, the highest since fixings began in 1989.

The real problem lay in the physical market where some companies reported difficulties with deliveries on spot contracts Wednesday and warned of multi-million dollar losses on short positions by some trade houses, traders said.
The shortage of metal forced dealers to stop quoting forward prices and led to a meeting of the 10 members London Platinum and Palladium Market Association.
"The members confirmed that there were no defaults in the market," association chairman Trevor Pitts said later.
"There may not have been any technical defaults, but there are certainly difficulties with deliveries," one U.S. refining source said.
"Members agreed to try to offer clients an orderly market in platinum and palladium but the key issue really depends on when the Russians begin exporting again," Pitts said.

Platinum and palladium users expected Russian supplies would have resumed by now, and have been borrowing the metal to cover their needs, but world inventories have been drawn down in the absence of Russian exports.
"To paraphrase the movie 'Jerry Maguire', its a case of 'show me the metal'," one NYMEX floor trader said said.
Russian officials told Japanese traders Wednesday that Russian PGM exports would resume on June 20, after a suspension since last December.
Analysts now believe Russia is moving from a marketing strategy based on Soviet-style production and export quotas to one based on getting the best prices and profits.
August gold rose $2 to $345.60 an ounce and July silver rose 7 cents to $4.77 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
